scenario: Today's main thread is that retrieval no longer stops at finding relevant passages and must also check whether the evidence holds up. PCG-RAG pins down which entity a question means before querying its attributes, and HiddenPathQA finds that question answering that walks a knowledge graph hop by hop goes astray when questions do not name the relations. ARMOR trains RAG models to answer correctly amid many noisy documents, and VisProve asks models to explain how each piece of evidence was used. DeepResearch RewardBench shows LLM judges often grade reports on dimensions outside the criteria, while SNAPRAG can extract the knowledge base behind a RAG system bit by bit. Alibaba's 1688, for its part, moves user behavioral evidence into search relevance tiers.

papers.title: Beyond Query-Item Matching: Personalized Behavioral Relevance Modeling for E-commerce Search via Rubric-Guided Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: E-commerce search systems typically separate query-item relevance matching from downstream personalized ranking. While effective for large-scale serving, this design leaves relevance levels dominated by objective query-item matching, forcing follow-up ranking to operate over candidate structures that may not reflect user behavioral preference. We define a new personalized behavioral relevance task, which predicts whether a relevance-stage candidate item is supported by the user’s behavioral evidence under current query intent. We develop a corresponding framework, BRIDGE, for Behavioral Relevance Inference with Dynamic Guidance from Evidence. It organizes multi-timescale behavioral context from online logs, obtains reliable supervision with multi-perspective annotation and adjudication, and trains an LLM to produce structured evidence-grounded decision rationales. It particularly incorporates sample-specific rubric rewards into GRPO to improve generated reasoning traces. Offline experiments validate that BRIDGE improves both prediction accuracy and reasoning quality. Online A/B tests show gains of 0.19% in active user-days and 0.67% in transaction-related user-days, both significant in statistics.
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Chenxu Wang, Jianzhi Shao, Jun Ji, Xiaozhou Xu, Zhe Sun, Wei Hu
papers.summary: E-commerce search usually has a relevance model sort candidates into tiers by text match between query and item, then hands them to a CTR model, so an item the user clearly prefers can get little exposure just because it landed in a low tier. This work from Alibaba's 1688 moves part of personalization into the relevance step: an LLM reads the user's same-day, recent and long-term search and purchase records, judges whether the item is backed by behavioral evidence, and if so promotes it one relevance tier. Training rewards not only the correct decision but also, through grading criteria generated for each sample, whether the reasoning actually uses that behavioral evidence. A three-day A/B test on 5% of main search traffic raised transaction-related user-days by 0.67%. ==Personalization need not live only in the ranking layer; changing relevance tiers also works.== Online serving only reads cached results computed offline, adding almost no latency.

papers.title: PCG-RAG: Progressive Compositional Grounding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Complex Web Question Answering
papers.authors: Linyao Zheng, Xuhang Shi, Zhifang Mao, Chongqi Qu, Xiuquan Hou
papers.abstract: Complex Web question answering requires retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems to identify target entities from multi-clue descriptions and connect evidence scattered across long Web pages. Individual pages often support only some of the required semantic constraints, while clues discovered on one page guide subsequent searches on others. However, premature reliance on partially supported entity hypotheses can divert retrieval from the original information need. RAG systems must therefore use partial evidence to guide further searches while seeking the evidence needed to establish the intended entities. We propose PCG-RAG, a novel RAG framework based on Progressive Compositional Grounding (PCG). Progressive Evidence Acquisition directs subsequent searches toward missing evidence for candidate attributes and relations. Compositional Reasoning separates candidate-guided retrieval from evidence-based answering along a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subquestions. Provisional names make dependent searches specific, while answering tasks use accepted results and unresolved identifying conditions, assessed against the original question. New passages connect the identifying clues to the requested relations, supporting evidence-based downstream answers. Evidence Grounding combines identifying and relational source passages with supported intermediate answers, connecting evidence across Web pages to the original conditions during final generation. On BrowseComp-Plus and WebWalkerQA, PCG-RAG improves accuracy over the leading compared baselines by 5.43 and 5.15 percentage points, respectively.
papers.summary: Complex web QA often requires first working out who or what several clues describe, then looking up an attribute of it, and a common mistake is to treat a name as settled after only one clue matches. The paper's example is a London power station converted into an art museum: a system that settles on Battersea from London and power station alone retrieves an architect who actually belongs to a different building. PCG-RAG treats such a partially matched name as a search lead, uses it to look up the conditions not yet satisfied, and lets later subquestions depend on it only once confirmed. At answer time it puts the passages that establish identity together with the passages that answer the attribute. On BrowseComp-Plus its accuracy beats the strongest baseline by 5.43 percentage points while using 82.98% fewer tokens. ==Pinning down the entity before querying its attributes beats piling on more retrieved results.==

papers.title: HiddenPathQA: A Benchmark for Knowledge Graph Question Answering When Questions Hide Their Paths
papers.abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) systems are typically evaluated on questions whose surface tokens lexically expose the gold KG path. Users, however, may ask questions without knowing the underlying schema: "Which condition could Andrew have due to family history?" compresses a 4-hop chain "Andrew --[father]--> parent --[father]--> grandparent --[medical condition]--> disease --[subclass of]--> hereditary disorder" into a single phrase (family history) that names none of those relations. We identify this collapse of path-question alignment as a blind spot in existing KGQA evaluation. Three major LLM-KG paradigms, hop-by-hop exploration, plan-then-retrieve, and similarity-based retrieval, implicitly rely on such lexical cues, an assumption rarely tested in practice. We make three contributions. (i) We introduce HiddenPathQA, a manually verified benchmark of 1,055 questions spanning 2-6 hops and multiple domains, constructed so that question wording does not reveal the gold path's relations. (ii) We propose Holistic Path Selection, which compares questions against candidate relation chains in the local subgraph as complete units, replacing irreversible per-hop relation scoring with globally informed chain-level reasoning. We develop two implementations, TieredHolistic and FlatHolistic. (iii) We conduct a pseudoword stress test that replaces entity names with meaningless placeholders to distinguish KG-grounded reasoning from entity-level memorization. Holistic Path Selection outperforms six strong KGQA baselines (ToG, PoG, FiDeLiS, R2-KG, KAPING, and KARPA) by 8.8-17.9 accuracy points across two LLM backbones and both original and pseudoword settings. Its advantage under pseudoword replacement shows that the gains cannot be explained by entity-level memorization alone.
papers.summary: Users ask questions without knowing the knowledge graph's structure. Asking which condition Andrew could have due to family history really means a multi-hop path through father, father's father, medical condition and hereditary disorder, yet the question names none of those relations. Existing KGQA test sets nearly spell the path out in the wording, so the three families of methods, picking relations hop by hop, planning then retrieving, and recalling by vector similarity, have rarely been tested on this case. The authors built over a thousand such questions and also replaced entity names with meaningless codes to rule out answering from memory: LLMs that do not query the graph drop about 40 points on the coded version, close to guessing. Their approach lists all candidate relation chains around the entity to the LLM at once for whole-chain comparison, with no pruning along the way. This approach beats six baselines by 8.8 to 17.9 points. ==The trouble with hop-by-hop scoring is that one wrong step midway cannot be undone.==

papers.title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77× fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.
papers.authors: Melih Coşğun, Mehmet Emre Gürsoy, Alptekin Küpçü, Sinem Sav
papers.summary: The private knowledge base behind a RAG system can be extracted one question at a time: the attacker appends an instruction to the query telling the model to repeat the retrieved documents verbatim, then builds the next batch of queries from what comes back. Existing attacks either have the attacker run a separate LLM to write queries or need many queries. SNAPRAG uses no LLM and instead swaps some tokens in already stolen text, so each new query lands far enough from seen content in the attacker's local embedding space to hit parts of the knowledge base not yet retrieved. To steal half a knowledge base, existing methods need up to 6.77 times as many queries. Within the same query budget it recovers up to 96.9% of the documents. When the targets add input and output moderation, it still leads on four of the five. ==Content moderation alone cannot stop an attack that extracts the data bit by bit.==

papers.title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs
papers.authors: Haoran Luo, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Linhao Luo, Yikai Guo, Qika Lin, Fangzhi Xu, Jiapu Wang, Xiaobao Wu, Yifan Zhu, Luu Anh Tuan
papers.abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.
papers.summary: Multimodal RAG carries two real costs: building the knowledge graph means paying an LLM to extract entities, and multi-round retrieval keeps stretching the context. MMGraph-Agent builds its graph simply: a local named-entity tool links the entities in each sentence into one hyperedge, an edge that can connect several entities at once. Images are encoded straight into the index with CLIP, so the whole build calls no paid API and finishes in a few CPU hours. At retrieval time it mimics a CPU's two-level cache, condensing each round's evidence into a digest in a small cache that later rounds reuse first. Across 23 multimodal QA datasets it beats the second-best method on each dataset by 11.6 F1 points on average, and the cache cuts token usage by 67%. ==Switching graph building to cheap rule-based extraction did not hurt quality.==

papers.title: DeepResearch RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Deep Research Report
papers.authors: Shudong Liu, Yuting Zhong, Guanhua Chen, Xinyi Yang, Junnan Liu, Lidia S. Chao, Jiaheng Liu, Derek F. Wong
papers.abstract: Empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs), deep research systems integrate online information into research reports through multi-step web searching and information synthesis. Evaluating these reports presents a significant challenge due to their long context, high information density, and domain specificity, necessitating the use of AI evaluation as a substitute for prohibitively expensive human assessment. However, few studies have examined the effectiveness of existing reward models or LLMs in understanding and evaluating such research reports. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepResearch RewardBench, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating reward modeling for research reports. We collect diverse report candidates from multiple agents or tool-augmented LLMs. These candidates are scored using query-specific golden rubrics, and we ensure data quality and difficulty through a combination of multi-round filtering and human verification. Our benchmark comprises preference datasets formatted as pairs, triplets, and quadruplets to test ranking capabilities across varying levels of difficulty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current reward models handle general coherence effectively, their performance significantly degrades when evaluating research reports. Generative LLMs acting as judges demonstrate comprehensive superiority in this domain, with comparative evaluation proving more effective than direct scoring methods. We anticipate that this benchmark will serve as a vital testbed for the evaluation and advancement of research agents.
papers.summary: Long reports written by deep research agents are too expensive for human review, so people score them with reward models or LLMs, yet few have systematically checked whether that works. The authors collected reports from several agents, ordered them by the original datasets' expert grading criteria, and grouped them into comparison items of two, three or four reports. Conventional reward models clearly struggle here, and LLMs used directly as judges do best. Having a judge compare several reports together is far more accurate than scoring each one alone, by 28.4 points on average when ranking four. When scoring alone, models keep giving 80 or 85, so good and bad reports blur together. Manual analysis of errors shows the most common mistake is the judge picking dimensions outside the grading criteria, such as caring more about how fresh the citations are or how many tables there are. ==Grading reports is hard because the judge's dimensions do not match the criteria.==

papers.title: Dhara: Evidence-Oriented Retrieval for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.abstract: Relevant evidence in Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) collections may be distributed across passages in different parts of a work, including verses, translations, and commentaries. Locating it requires matching natural-language questions and partially remembered verse fragments to source passages. We present Dhara, a retrieval engine combining hybrid search, chapter- and book-level Entity Notes (EN), Fuzzy Verse Retrieval (FVR), and neural reranking. Five comparisons on the 325 questions in Dhara Bench examine retrieval representations against BM25, EN's contribution, reranker quality and computation time, FVR, and Gemini. BGE-M3 single-vector retrieval exceeds BM25 in nDCG@10, Recall@20, and MRR@20 across all categories. Its scores are broadly comparable to ColBERTv2, with mean retrieval times of 0.108 s and 0.962 s under the same hardware configuration and a smaller memory footprint for chunk storage on disk. Adding EN to a direct branch with a matched candidate count improves nDCG@10 in all twelve categories with Qwen and ten with BGE; the combined ranking is capped at the same candidate count. Qwen improves nDCG@10, Precision@5, and MRR@20 over BGE in every category, at approximately 6.72 times the overall estimated serial computation time. FVR increases Verse-category nDCG@10 by approximately 20 percentage points with either reranker. Gemini is evaluated after source mapping and manual review with relevance annotations visible. The Qwen pipeline with EN and FVR has higher Recall@20 than Gemini in ten categories and stronger complete-evidence retrieval in Multi-hop questions, while Gemini retains early-relevance advantages in several categories. The results inform retrieval choices according to evidence requirements and resource budgets.
papers.authors: Avinash Holenarasipur Nagendra, Anand Kaniyaar Sriranga Prasad, Rahul Vishwakarma, Trupti Gavit, Anish Amol Tipnis, Yashaswini Mandayam Rangayyan, Vinod Appajanna, Kousik Sarathy Sridharan, Mohan Raghavan
papers.summary: Finding evidence in Indian classical texts is hard because answers are often spread across verses, translations and commentaries in different places, and askers often remember only half a line of a verse. Besides standard hybrid retrieval, Dhara adds two routes. One writes notes in advance on the people and concepts in each chapter and book, then follows links from a matched note back to source passages. The other pulls verse fragments out of the question for fuzzy matching. Fragment matching raises nDCG@10 on verse questions by about 20 percentage points. Single-vector retrieval performs close to multi-vector ColBERTv2, yet its mean retrieval time is 0.108 s against 0.962 s, with a smaller disk footprint. A stronger reranker does better on every question type, at the cost of several times more total computation time. ==For multi-passage questions, what matters is finding the full set at once, not only whether the first hit is right.==

papers.title: Cascading Circle Loss: Order-Preserving Contrastive Learning for Graded Legal Retrieval
papers.summary: Legal retrieval must find not only the clause that directly answers, but also rank related definitions, liability caps and force majeure clauses behind it by degree of relevance, while the common InfoNCE only separates relevant from irrelevant and ignores order among positives. CasCL splits these two jobs, with InfoNCE comparing only the most relevant passage against negatives to separate relevant from irrelevant. A second loss strings the graded passages into a chain by score, with the hardest negatives at the end, and requires each level to sit closer to the query than the next by a gap proportional to the score difference. Getting each adjacent pair right then orders the whole chain. On the company's contract clause data in six languages, its NDCG@10 beats Circle Loss by 2.94 points, and removing InfoNCE drops Recall@1 from 41.14 to 28.56. ==Each loss handles one job, and dropping either one hurts.== The intermediate relevance levels were labeled by a vote of three LLMs and were not compared against human labels.

papers.title: VisProve: Learning Typed Visual Provenance for Scientific Document Question Answering
papers.authors: Jingxuan Wei, Zhengyang Wang, Zheng Guo, Xiaoming Wu, Fuqiang Wang, Xin Wang, Bihui Yu, Yining Wang, Junnan Zhu
papers.abstract: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.
papers.summary: Citations in scientific paper QA today mostly box where an answer comes from but not how that content is used: read off directly, condensed, or reached only by reasoning. The authors built nearly four thousand QA items over full papers, labeling each piece of evidence with its page, section, region box and one of these three uses. As the model generates each token, VisProve first predicts which region to look at and reads the visual features there, then estimates which use that evidence serves, adding both back into generation as a small bounded correction. Against plain supervised fine-tuning on the same backbone, section-level F1 rises from 45.99 to 53.24 while page-level localization barely moves. The F1 that requires both region and use to match is still only 5.48. ==Models mostly find the right page, but are far from explaining how each piece of evidence supports the answer.==

papers.title: ARMOR: Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise-Robust RAG Reasoning
papers.authors: Yan Wang, Yuxin Zhang, Shenyu Zhang, Yongrui Chen, Sheng Bi, Guilin Qi
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.
papers.summary: Retrieved documents always carry irrelevant or even misleading content, and to withstand that noise a RAG model needs three skills at once: knowing whether it already knows the answer, picking out useful documents, and reasoning to an answer amid noise. Training all three together with reinforcement learning makes their rewards interfere. ARMOR trains only one skill per round, with a scheduler picking whichever skill's score changed most recently. It also changes how GRPO computes advantages: because the subtasks have small output spaces, repeated samples for the same question are often very similar and cannot be told apart within the group, so it normalizes across the whole batch instead. When the authors mix noise into five retrieved documents, even at 80% noise, its correctness stays at 69%. Training the three skills in a fixed order instead makes the model forget what it learned earlier. ==Letting training order follow the model's progress is steadier than fixing it in advance.==
